predecessors.name: Chichen Itza
predecessors.text: 'The primary city in a group of allies' covering 'much of northern Yucatan'; the page names no provinces and no frontier, so the state of Yucatan is the researcher's reading

successors.name: Maya city-states (Postclassic)
successors.text: 'The primary city in a group of allies' covering 'much of northern Yucatan'; the page names no provinces and no frontier, so the state of Yucatan is the researcher's reading

successors.name: Tutul Xiu
successors.text: Maní, the Xiu capital; the page gives no extent

successors.name: Sotuta
successors.text: Sotuta, the Cocom province, 'landlocked, north of Maní'; the pages give no extent

successors.name: Cupul
successors.text: 'Cupul's former capital is the site of modern Valladolid'; 'one of the most extensive and densely populated Maya provinces' (Cupul page)

successors.name: Ah Kin Chel
successors.text: Tecoh, the capital, is 'near Izamal'; the page names no other town

successors.name: Ceh Pech
successors.text: Motul, 'the capital of the principality named after the family'; 'a province, or kuchkabal, of the northern Yucatán Peninsula'; 25 towns in 1567

successors.name: Chikinchel
successors.text: 'Chikinchel was a Mayan chiefdom on the northern coast of the Yucatán'; the page gives bounds, not a centre

successors.name: Cochuah
successors.text: Tihosuco, the capital; 'bordered with Cupul in the north, with Sotuta, Tutul Xiu and Chakán Putún in the west' and 'great forests with little population up to the Bay of Ascension'

successors.name: Chakan
successors.text: Ti'ho (T'ho), the capital, on the site of Mérida

successors.name: Ah Canul
successors.text: Calkini, the capital, in the 'northwest Yucatán Peninsula'; 'Ah Canul was divided into eight batabilob'

successors.name: Can Pech
successors.text: 'Can Pech was south of Ah Canul and north of Chakán Putum, on the coast of the Gulf of Mexico'; 'Most of Campeche's population lived near the coast'

successors.name: Ekab
successors.text: Ekab on the 'northeastern Yucatán Peninsula': its coastal ports from Tulum to Cape Catoche; neighbours Chikinchel, Tazes, Cupul and Cochuah to the west, Uaymil to the south

successors.name: Chakán Putum
successors.text: 'the territory lay on the Champotón River, with the Gulf of Mexico to the west'; 'Modern Champotón ... was built on the site of the capital'

successors.name: Kowoj
successors.text: The Kowoj 'reconstructed ... social boundaries' around the Yaxha lagoon (Topoxte), east of Lake Petén Itzá; the page gives no extent

ledger.x: 1220s: Mayapan becomes the capital of the Maya of Yucatan; 'some sources date a revolt against Chichen Itza's Maya-Toltec lords to 1221', after which 'the lords built a new capital near Telchaquillo'; the Cocom chief 'was chosen to be king'.

1221: page silent on the year the alliance formed; Mayapan leads 'a group of allies that included much of the northern Yucatan' which 'lasted for over 200 years'; Hunac Ceel is 'the general who defeated the rulers of Chichen Itza'.

1441: 'In 1441, Ah Xiu Xupan of the powerful noble family of Xiu' organised a revolt and 'all of the Cocom family, except one ... were killed'; 'written records state that the site was abandoned in A.D.

wars.name: Xiu revolt against Mayapan
wars.outcome: Ah Xiu Xupan's revolt killed the Cocom family but one and ended Mayapan; 'Yucatan devolved into warring city-states'.

wars.name: Hunac Ceel's war on Chichen Itza
wars.outcome: Chronicle tradition only: Hunac Ceel 'conquered Chichen Itza in the 13th century' (Chichen Itza page) / 'defeated the rulers of Chichen Itza' (Mayapan page); archaeology puts Chichen Itza's decline before 1100, so no contest is drawn.

certainty.note: The confederacy has no described frontier.
